# 1. The survey

In 2025, the people around the BioHackathon in Japan, run by the Database Center for Life
Science (DBCLS), were asked how they use AI in their work. 105 answered, in English, Japanese or Thai. The questions cover how often they
use it, for which tasks and how much of each task they hand over, what goes wrong, how
satisfied they are, what their institution provides, and five concerns.

The answers are public, free to reuse for any purpose (CC0):

- **The data:** GigaDB, <https://doi.org/10.5524/102783>
- **The article that describes it:** Sriwichai et al. (2026), *AI in practice: a
  multilingual survey of 2025 BioHackathon participants*, GigaByte,
  <https://doi.org/10.46471/gigabyte.179>

The files are in `data/survey/` in your SIRE516 project folder (the one with
`SIRE516.Rproj`), unchanged from GigaDB, and the code below reads them from there. If your
folder has no `data/survey/`, download the course folder again into a new folder, so your
own files stay in the old one, and work in the new one from now on. Two GigaDB files are
not included: an `.xlsx` that is the same table as the cleaned `.csv`, and a short readme,
whose licence and citation are given above.

Three of the files matter most:

| File | What it holds |
|---|---|
| `…_data_cleaned_ENG_R1.csv` | One row per person, in English. **The table you analyse.** |
| `…_cleaned_codebook_ENG_R1.csv` | What each column of that table means |
| `…_GoogleForms.pdf` | The questionnaire itself: every question, every option, and which question each person was sent to next |

The rest:

- `…_raw_anon_ENG_v1.csv`: the answers before cleaning, with the long written answers kept
- `…_original_languages_R1.csv`: each answer in the language it was given in
- `Translation_lookup_table_R1.csv`: each answer option in English, Thai and Japanese
- `README_R1.md`: the authors' own notes on the data, worth reading once. Some file names,
  folders and counts in it differ from the files here; the files are right

**Open the questionnaire PDF now and keep it open.** Almost every question was optional,
and some were shown only to some people. When a cell is blank, the questionnaire tells you
whether that person was ever shown the question. If they were, the blank alone cannot tell
you why.

The article summarises the table in one figure:

![](https://gigabytejournal.com/admin/apis/public/article_shell/uploads/article_files/Gigabyte/Gigabyte/2026/gigabyte179/gigabyte-2026-179-g001.jpg)

<small>Figure 1 of Sriwichai et al. (2026), GigaByte, CC BY 4.0.</small>

Today you rebuild it, one panel at a time. That is the project's first step: before you
ask the data a new question, reproduce what has already been reported from it. Each panel
turns out to teach something about the table.

---

# 2. Read it, and look

```{r}
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)

survey <- read_csv("data/survey/Biohackathon2025AISurvey_data_cleaned_ENG_R1.csv",
                   show_col_types = FALSE)
dim(survey)
```

105 rows, one per person. 33 columns: one for each question or part of one (the task
question has a column for each of its seven tasks), plus seven that hold what people wrote
under *Other*. Not every question made it into the table. The language each person
answered in, for one, is not there.

*Predict:* the five `concern_` columns are scores from 1 to 5. What type should `glimpse()`
show for them?

```{r}
glimpse(survey)
```

Four are `<dbl>`, numbers. `concern_misinfo` is `<chr>`, text. Look at its values:

```{r}
count(survey, concern_misinfo)
```

<details>
<summary>**`count()`** — how many rows have each value</summary>

`count(survey, concern_misinfo)` is short for

```r
survey |>
  group_by(concern_misinfo) |>
  summarise(n = n())
```

the group-and-count from Class 5. Add `sort = TRUE` to put the largest group first. Give
it two columns, `count(table, a, b)`, and it counts each combination.

</details>

Two of the answers kept their label: `5 - Very concerned` and `1 - Not concerned at all`.
Every value in a column has the same type, so one piece of text makes the whole column
text. `mean()` of it returns `NA` with a warning. `parse_number()` keeps the number at the
start of each value:

```{r}
survey <- survey |>
  mutate(concern_misinfo = parse_number(concern_misinfo))

count(survey, concern_misinfo)
```

<details>
<summary>**`parse_number()`** — the number inside a piece of text</summary>

From `readr`. It drops everything before the first number and everything after it:
`parse_number("5 - Very concerned")` is 5, and `parse_number("$1,200")` is 1200. Values
with no number become `NA`, and it warns you how many.

</details>

Section 6 comes back to this column. It is more interesting than it looks.

The codebook says what each column holds:

```{r}
codebook <- read_csv("data/survey/Biohackathon2025AISurvey_cleaned_codebook_ENG_R1.csv",
                     show_col_types = FALSE)

codebook |>
  select(clean_column_name, description) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

<details>
<summary>**`knitr::kable()`** — a table as a formatted table</summary>

A tibble prints as text, and cuts long values short. `kable()` prints a table as a
formatted table in the knitted page, every value in full. It changes how the table looks,
not what it holds. `knitr::` calls a function from the `knitr` package without loading it
with `library()`.

</details>

Columns ending in `_other_text` hold what people wrote when they picked *Other*. Several
columns hold more than one answer per person; section 5 deals with those.

---

# 3. Panel A: how often people use AI

```{r}
count(survey, ai_use_level, sort = TRUE)
```

61 of 105 chose *I use AI everyday*; one chose *I never use AI*. The AI researchers and
developers answered with a role rather than a frequency.

`ggplot()` would put these bars in alphabetical order. To draw them in the article's
order, turn the column into a **factor**: text with its possible values, its *levels*, in
a fixed order. Type the levels as the questionnaire words them:

```{r}
typed <- c("I never use AI", "I am an AI developer", "I am an AI researcher",
           "I use AI a few times a month", "I use AI a few times a week",
           "I use AI everyday", "Other")
```

*Predict:* every person should land in one of the seven levels. Do they?

```{r}
count(survey, use = factor(ai_use_level, levels = typed))
```

<details>
<summary>**`factor()`** — text with a fixed set of values, in a fixed order</summary>

`factor(x, levels = ...)` keeps the values of `x` and records their order. Plots, tables
and `count()` follow that order instead of the alphabet. A plot draws the first level
nearest the origin, so on a y-axis the first level sits at the bottom. That is why `typed`
starts with *never*.

Any value of `x` that does not match a level **exactly** becomes `NA`, without a warning.

Inside `count()`, `use = factor(...)` makes the new column first and counts it, as
`mutate()` would.

</details>

14 people became `NA`, and nothing warned you. The 6 researchers and the 8 people who use
AI a few times a month are gone. Ask the data what it actually holds:

```{r}
unique(survey$ai_use_level)
```

`unique()` lists each different value once.

Look closely at `I use Al a few times a month` and `I am an Al researcher`. That is *Al*,
with a lower-case L, not *AI*. In many fonts, including the one in the plots, the two look the same.
The questionnaire says AI, the cleaned table says Al, and `factor()` matches exactly.
**Copy values from the data, never from the questionnaire.**

```{r}
use_levels <- c("I never use AI", "I am an AI developer",
                "I am an Al researcher",            # Al, lower-case L, as in the data
                "I use Al a few times a month",     # here too
                "I use AI a few times a week", "I use AI everyday", "Other")

survey <- survey |>
  mutate(use = factor(ai_use_level, levels = use_levels))

count(survey, use)
```

No `NA`. Now the panel; the article leaves out the two *Other* answers:

```{r}
survey |>
  filter(use != "Other") |>
  ggplot(aes(y = use)) +
  geom_bar() +
  labs(x = "Respondents", y = NULL)
```

The same as the article's panel A.

---

# 4. Panel B: where they work

```{r}
countries <- count(survey, country, sort = TRUE)
countries
```

*Predict:* the article shows the countries with more than one respondent. How many rows
will `filter(countries, n > 1)` keep?

```{r}
filter(countries, n > 1)
```

Ten, not the article's nine. The extra row is `NA`: 6 people left the country blank, or wrote
something that is not a country and was cleared when the table was cleaned. Drop it, and
draw:

```{r}
countries |>
  filter(n > 1, !is.na(country)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = n, y = reorder(country, n))) +
  geom_col() +
  labs(x = "Respondents", y = NULL)
```

The same as panel B. Read it for what it means for your project: 67 of the 105 work in
Japan or Thailand, Germany has 10, and 6 gave no country. The remaining 22 are spread
thinly: no other country has more than 4 people. A comparison between countries is, in practice, Japan against
Thailand, with everyone else as a mixed third group. Decide what to do with the 6 who gave
no country.

---

# 5. Panel C: what people use AI for, and how much

The task question is a grid: seven tasks, and for each one, three boxes.

- **Complete:** *I use AI to complete the entire task with little to no editing*
- **Draft:** *I use AI to generate a first draft, which I then edit and finalize*
- **Assist:** *I use AI to assist with specific parts of a task*

It says *Check all that apply*, so a cell can hold more than one box, joined by `", "`.
Put the seven task columns into one long table, as in Class 5:

```{r}
tasks <- survey |>
  select(starts_with("task_")) |>
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "task", values_to = "answer")

dim(tasks)
```

105 people × 7 tasks = 735 rows. `starts_with("task_")` picks the columns whose names start
with `task_`, and `everything()` picks every column there is: here, all seven.

To count the boxes, the obvious move is to split each cell at its commas, one answer per
row, and count the answers.

*Predict:* how many different answers will that give?

```{r}
tasks |>
  filter(!is.na(answer)) |>
  separate_longer_delim(answer, delim = ", ") |>
  count(answer)
```

<details>
<summary>**`separate_longer_delim()`** — one row per piece of a cell</summary>

From `tidyr`. `separate_longer_delim(answer, delim = ", ")` cuts each value of `answer`
wherever `", "` appears and gives each piece its own row; the other columns are copied
down. It is the right tool when no answer contains the separator. Here one does.

</details>

Four, not three. *Which I then edit and finalize* is not an answer. It is the second half
of the Draft box, which contains a comma itself, so the split cut it in two. Every Draft
box was counted twice: 280 under each half. Nothing errored.

The same trap waits in three more columns, where an answer contains a comma:

- `improvements_desired`: *Privacy, security & ethics*
- `challenges_faced`: *Data limitations (size, quality, accessibility)* and *Lack of
  institutional support (software, hardware, guidance)*
- `inst_support_types`: *Access to institutional AI software or platforms (licenses,
  subscriptions)*

So ask each cell a yes-or-no question instead: **does it contain this box's text?**

```{r}
tasks <- tasks |>
  mutate(complete = grepl("complete the entire task", answer, fixed = TRUE),
         draft    = grepl("generate a first draft", answer, fixed = TRUE),
         assist   = grepl("assist with specific parts", answer, fixed = TRUE))

tasks |>
  filter(!is.na(answer)) |>
  group_by(task) |>
  summarise(answered = n(), assist = sum(assist), draft = sum(draft),
            complete = sum(complete))
```

<details>
<summary>**`grepl()`** — does this text appear in each value?</summary>

`grepl("first draft", x, fixed = TRUE)` returns TRUE or FALSE for each value of `x`: does
it contain *first draft*? A blank (`NA`) gives FALSE. `sum()` of the result counts the
TRUEs, as in Class 4.

`fixed = TRUE` means *match these characters exactly*. Without it, characters such as
`(` `)` `.` `+` are pattern symbols, not text. Search for
`"Lack of institutional support (software, hardware, guidance)"` without `fixed = TRUE`
and it matches nobody: not an error, a count of 0. With it, 17 people.

Match a phrase that only the box you want contains: *complete the entire task* appears in
nothing but the Complete box.

</details>

Now compare with the article's panel C. Assist matches in every row. Draft and Complete
mostly do not: coding, for example, has 51 drafters and 16 completers here, 40 and 11 in the
article.

The article says people indicated whether they used AI "primarily" to assist, draft or
complete: one answer per task. But the form let people tick several, and some did. Count the cells with more than one box (TRUE counts as 1, so the three columns add up
to the number of boxes):

```{r}
tasks |>
  filter(assist + draft + complete > 1) |>
  count(task)
```

The article's numbers come back if each person is counted **once** per task, under the
lightest use they ticked: Assist if they ticked it, otherwise Draft, otherwise Complete.

```{r}
tasks |>
  filter(!is.na(answer)) |>
  mutate(mode = case_when(assist ~ "Assist",
                          draft ~ "Draft",
                          complete ~ "Complete")) |>
  count(task, mode) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = mode, values_from = n) |>
  select(task, Assist, Draft, Complete)
```

<details>
<summary>**`case_when()`** — the first condition that is TRUE wins</summary>

From `dplyr`. Each line is `condition ~ value`. For each row, `case_when()` takes the
value of the first line whose condition is TRUE, so the order of the lines is the rule.
A row where no line is TRUE gets `NA`.

</details>

All 21 numbers match the article's table. Its percentages divide by 105, so a blank cell
counts as not using AI for that task. The dataset's `README_R1.md` warns that a blank
could also mean the task does not apply to that person, or that they skipped the
question.

Neither way of counting is wrong. They answer different questions: *how many people let AI
draft their code?* is 51; *how many people's lightest use of AI for code is drafting?* is
40. Every figure you make for the project rests on choices like these. Write yours down.

---

# 6. Panel D: what people worry about

Put the five concern columns into one long table, and take each one's mean, as the article
did:

```{r}
concern <- survey |>
  select(starts_with("concern_")) |>
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "issue", values_to = "score")

concern |>
  group_by(issue) |>
  summarise(answered = sum(!is.na(score)),
            mean = round(mean(score, na.rm = TRUE), 2)) |>
  arrange(desc(mean))
```

Every number matches panel D. Misinformation tops the list by three quarters of a
point.

*Predict:* before you write that sentence in a report, what would you look at?

The answers under each mean. Plot them:

```{r, fig.width = 9, fig.height = 3}
concern |>
  filter(!is.na(score)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = score)) +
  geom_bar() +
  facet_wrap(~ issue, nrow = 1) +
  labs(x = "Concern (1 = not concerned at all, 5 = very concerned)", y = "People")
```

`nrow = 1` puts the five panels in one row. Every panel uses the same scales, so the
empty places at 1 and 5 line up.

And count them, blanks included:

```{r}
concern |>
  count(issue, score) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = score, values_from = n, values_fill = 0, names_sort = TRUE)
```

`values_fill = 0` writes 0 where a combination never occurs, instead of `NA`.
`names_sort = TRUE` puts the new columns in order, 1 to 5, then the blanks.

Four of the five issues have **no 1s and no 5s at all**. Only misinformation uses the
whole scale, and 49 people gave it a 5.

Question 21 of the questionnaire is a single grid: the five issues are its rows, and every
row has the same five boxes, 1 to 5. Out of 76 people who rated bias, not one picked 5,
while 49 of 95 picked 5 for misinformation on the same grid. And the blanks run high
for exactly those four: 29 to 41 of 105, against 10 for misinformation.

One explanation fits both: answers in the two end boxes were lost from four of the five
columns before the file was published, and became `NA`. Test it. A lost answer would show
up as a blank, so the blanks should fall on the people likeliest to have picked an end
box. Assume that people with a strong view on one issue often hold strong views on
others; this table cannot show it, since the strong views are what went missing. Then
those people are the ones with a strong view on misinformation. Group people by their
misinformation answer:

```{r}
survey |>
  mutate(blanks = is.na(concern_bias) + is.na(concern_privacy) +
                  is.na(concern_ip) + is.na(concern_environment)) |>
  filter(!is.na(concern_misinfo)) |>
  group_by(concern_misinfo) |>
  summarise(people = n(), left_any_blank = sum(blanks > 0))
```

Blanks climb with the misinformation answer: 1 of the 5 who gave it a 2, against 38 of
the 49 who gave it a 5. Only one person gave it a 1, too few to say anything about the low
end. The climb fits lost end answers.

Very concerned people skipping more rows would also give a climb. Skipping does not
explain the first finding, though: among the 76 bias answers that are there, not one is a
5. For that, every person who would have picked 5 must have skipped the row.

The files cannot settle it. The dataset's README treats a blank concern answer as a
non-response whose reason cannot be determined. Treat lost end answers as the likeliest reading, not as a
fact. One more detail fits it: where the 1s and 5s did survive, they kept their labels,
*1 - Not concerned at all* and *5 - Very concerned*, and the labels are why section 2
found that column stored as text. **The column that looked broken is the one that kept
its 1s and 5s.**

<details>
<summary>**How sure is this?** The same pattern, by the language people answered in</summary>

The original-language file holds each answer as it was given, in English, Japanese or
Thai, in the same row order as the cleaned table. The lookup table lists every answer
option in all three languages, so joining the AI-use answer to it gives each person's
language:

```{r}
original <- read_csv(
  "data/survey/Biohackathon2025AISurvey_data_raw_anon_original_languages_R1.csv",
  show_col_types = FALSE)

options <- read_csv("data/survey/Translation_lookup_table_R1.csv",
                    show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "language", values_to = "text")

# column 7 of the original file is the AI-use question
form <- tibble(text = original[[7]]) |>
  left_join(options, by = "text")

dim(form)

survey |>
  mutate(language = form$language) |>
  count(language, concern_misinfo) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = concern_misinfo, values_from = n, values_fill = 0,
              names_sort = TRUE)
```

`original[[7]]` takes column 7 as a vector. `$` would need the column's name, and here
the name is the whole question. The two `NA` languages are the two people who answered
*Other* in their own words.

On the English and Japanese forms, 48 of 83 people gave misinformation a 5, and one left
it blank. On the Thai form: no 1s, no 5s, and 9 blanks out of 20.

Could that be people in Thailand answering differently, rather than the form? Take only
the people who work in Thailand, and split them by the form they chose:

```{r}
survey |>
  mutate(language = form$language) |>
  filter(country == "Thailand") |>
  count(language, concern_misinfo)
```

Same country, different form. On the English form, 3 of 7 gave misinformation a 5 and
none left it blank. On the Thai form, none gave a 5 and 7 of 16 left it blank. People
chose their form, so the two groups may differ in other ways, and the numbers are small.
But it is what you would see if the Thai form lost its end answers, and country alone
does not explain it.

</details>

What this does to panel D, if the reading is right: a mean of 2s, 3s and 4s can never be
above 4. For four of the five issues, the most and the least concerned would be missing
from the mean. Misinformation may rank first partly because it is the only issue whose 5s
were kept, on two of the three forms.

For the project: the four concern columns other than `concern_misinfo` cannot give you a
mean, a ranking, or a comparison you can defend. `concern_misinfo` shows no sign of the
problem among the people who answered in English or Japanese.

---

# 7. The rest of the table

Satisfaction and institutional support have no missing ends. Both run from 1 to 5, and
their blanks are few:

```{r}
count(survey, satisfaction_score)
count(survey, inst_support_score)
```

Satisfaction's one blank is the person who never uses AI, who was never asked; support
has three.

Some blanks are there by design. Question 18, *what would AI tools need to improve*, was
only shown to people who rated their satisfaction 1, 2 or 3:

```{r}
survey |>
  group_by(satisfaction_score) |>
  summarise(people = n(), answered_q18 = sum(!is.na(improvements_desired)))
```

Nobody who gave a 4 or a 5 answered it, because nobody who gave a 4 or a 5 saw it. Of the
question's 71 blanks, 70 are people who were never asked: the 69 who gave a 4 or a 5, and
the one person who never uses AI, whom the questionnaire sent past every AI question.
Check the questionnaire before you read a blank as anything.

Which tools people named. People were asked to separate them with commas, and no tool
name contains one, so splitting at the commas is safe here:

```{r}
survey |>
  filter(!is.na(ai_tools_used)) |>
  separate_longer_delim(ai_tools_used, delim = ", ") |>
  count(ai_tools_used, sort = TRUE)
```

77 people named at least one tool, and 63 of them named ChatGPT.

## Try it: the challenges

`challenges_faced` holds the boxes each person ticked at question 15: nine named
challenges, plus *Other*. Count how many people ticked each named challenge, and draw it.

Two of the boxes contain commas, and two others are spelled with *Al* in the cleaned
table. Match a short phrase that only one box contains.

<details>
<summary>**One answer**</summary>

```{r}
challenges <- survey |>
  summarise(
    inaccurate     = sum(grepl("inaccurate or unreliable", challenges_faced, fixed = TRUE)),
    over_reliance  = sum(grepl("Over-reliance", challenges_faced, fixed = TRUE)),
    ethics_privacy = sum(grepl("Ethical or privacy", challenges_faced, fixed = TRUE)),
    data_limits    = sum(grepl("Data limitations", challenges_faced, fixed = TRUE)),
    compute_cost   = sum(grepl("computational cost", challenges_faced, fixed = TRUE)),
    integrating    = sum(grepl("existing workflows", challenges_faced, fixed = TRUE)),
    no_support     = sum(grepl("Lack of institutional support", challenges_faced,
                               fixed = TRUE)),
    hard_to_read   = sum(grepl("difficult to interpret", challenges_faced, fixed = TRUE)),
    too_complex    = sum(grepl("too complex", challenges_faced, fixed = TRUE))
  ) |>
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "challenge", values_to = "people")

challenges

ggplot(challenges, aes(x = people, y = reorder(challenge, people))) +
  geom_col() +
  labs(x = "People who ticked it", y = NULL)
```

77 of the 101 people who answered ticked *outputs are inaccurate or unreliable*.

</details>

---

# 8. Where to take it

The project asks a question of this table that the article does not answer. Some that it
can support:

- Who is most satisfied with AI: everyday users or occasional ones? Those with more
  institutional support? `lm()` from Class 7 gives a first answer to both, treating the
  1–5 score as a number: a difference in average satisfaction between groups, or a change
  per point of support.
- Does institutional support differ between Japan, Thailand and everywhere else?
- Do the people who report inaccurate output rate their satisfaction lower?
- Do people hand more of their coding to AI than their writing? 89 people answered both,
  so you can compare them person by person. Decide first what a blank, and a cell with
  several boxes, will mean.
- Which challenges go with which tasks?

Before you choose, know what this table is:

- **105 people who chose to answer**, around one hackathon. It describes them, not
  bioinformaticians in general.
- **Small groups.** 6 AI researchers, 4 AI developers, 1 person who never uses AI.
  A group of 4 gives a mean, but a weak one.
- **Almost every question optional.** Count the blanks in every column you use, and check
  the questionnaire for why they are there.
- **The concern columns.** Four have no 1s or 5s, most likely lost, and so does
  `concern_misinfo` on the Thai form (section 6).
- **Country and form go together.** Most people in Thailand answered on the Thai form, and
  section 6 found signs that the form changed what was recorded. A difference between
  countries may be a difference between forms.

> **Before you trust a summary of this survey, look at the answers under it.**
